explanation: A mock integration in API Gateway lets the developer define canned responses for each status code directly in the integration/method response configuration, without any backend (Lambda, HTTP endpoint, etc.) existing yet, so other teams can immediately start testing against the API's contract. Request validators check incoming payload structure but don't generate response bodies for testing. A gateway response customizes API Gateway's own error responses (like 403 or 404), not arbitrary method responses for a resource. A Lambda authorizer controls access to the API and has nothing to do with generating test responses.

question: A company is releasing a new feature. Users can request early access to the new feature by using an application form. The company expects a surge of requests when the application form becomes available. Each request will be stored as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Each item will contain the user's username, the submission date, and a validation status of UNVALIDATED. VALID, or NOT VALID. Each item also will contain the user's rating of the process on a scale of 1 to 5. Each user can submit one request. For the DynamoDB table, the developer must choose a partition key that will give the workload well-distributed records across partitions. Which DynamoDB attribute will meet these requirements?

options.text: Username
Submission date
Validation status
Rating of the process on a scale of 1 to 5

explanation: Since each user can submit only one request, using the username as the partition key produces a high-cardinality, evenly distributed key across a large and growing surge of unique users, spreading traffic across many partitions. Submission date would cluster all requests made on the same day (especially during a launch surge) onto a small number of partition values, creating hot partitions. Validation status and rating are extremely low-cardinality attributes (only 3 and 5 possible values respectively), which would concentrate items into very few partitions and severely limit throughput.

question: A developer is creating a publicly accessible enterprise website consisting of only static assets. The developer is hosting the website in Amazon S3 and serving the website to users through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The users of this application must not be able to access the application content directly from an S3 bucket. All content must be served through the Amazon CloudFront distribution. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a new origin access control (OAC) in CloudFront. Configure the CloudFront distribution's origin to use the new OAC. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow CloudFront OAC with read and write access to access Amazon S3 as the origin.

Update the S3 bucket settings. Enable the block all public access setting in Amazon S3. Configure the CloudFront distribution's with Amazon S3 as the origin. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow CloudFront write access.
Update the S3 bucket's static website settings. Enable static website hosting and specifying index and error documents. Update the CloudFront origin to use the S3 bucket's website endpoint.

Update the CloudFront distribution's origin to send a custom header. Update the S3 bucket policy with a condition by using the aws:RequestTag/tag-key key. Configure the tag-key as the custom header name, and the value being matched is the header's value.

explanation: Origin Access Control (OAC) lets CloudFront sign requests to S3 using SigV4, and updating the S3 bucket policy to allow only that CloudFront distribution's OAC to access the bucket (while keeping the bucket otherwise private) ensures users cannot bypass CloudFront and hit the S3 REST endpoint directly. Enabling static website hosting exposes a public S3 website endpoint that does not support OAC/OAI-based access restriction, so it cannot be locked down to CloudFront-only access. Simply blocking public access without configuring OAC in the distribution's origin leaves CloudFront without a way to authenticate to the private bucket. Relying on a custom header plus an aws:RequestTag condition is not how S3 bucket policies validate CloudFront-origin requests; that pattern doesn't map to a supported access-restriction mechanism.

question: A developer built an application that calls an external API to obtain data, processes the data, and saves the result to Amazon S3. The developer built a container image with all of the necessary dependencies to run the application as a container. The application runs locally and requires minimal CPU and RAM resources. The developer has created an Amazon ECS cluster. The developer needs to run the application hourly in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of infrastructure management overhead?

options.text: Add a capacity provider to manage instances.
Add an Amazon EC2 instance that runs the application.
Define a task definition with an AWS Fargate launch type.
Create an Amazon ECS cluster and add the managed node groups feature to run the application.

explanation: Defining an ECS task definition with the AWS Fargate launch type lets ECS run the small, infrequent (hourly) containerized job without the developer having to provision, patch, or scale any EC2 instances, since Fargate manages the underlying compute entirely. Adding a capacity provider to manage EC2 instances, launching a standalone EC2 instance, or configuring managed node groups (an EKS concept, not ECS) all require the developer to own instance lifecycle management, which is exactly the operational overhead Fargate eliminates for this lightweight, low-resource, periodic workload.

question: A company runs its website on AWS. The company posts daily polls on its website and publishes the poll results next day. The website stores user responses in an Amazon DynamoDB table. After the poll results are published, the company does not need to keep the user responses. A developer needs to implement a solution that will automatically remove old user responses from the DynamoDB table. The developer adds a new expiration_date attribute to the DynamoDB table. The developer plans to use the expiration_date attribute for the automation. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function to delete old user responses based on the expiration_date attribute. Create an Amazon EventBridge schedule to run the Lambda function daily.

Create an AWS Fargate task in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to delete old user responses based on the expiration_date attribute. Create an Amazon EventBridge schedule to run the Fargate task daily.
Create an AWS Glue job to delete old user responses based on the expiration_date attribute. Create an AWS Glue trigger schedule to run the job daily.
Enable TTL on the DynamoDB table and specify the expiration_date attribute. Expire old user responses by using DynamoDB TTL.

explanation: DynamoDB's built-in TTL feature automatically deletes items once their expiration_date attribute passes, using an internal background process that requires no application code, no scheduled compute, and no additional AWS resources to maintain, making it the lowest-effort option by far. Building a Lambda function, Fargate task, or Glue job with a daily EventBridge/Glue trigger all require writing and maintaining custom deletion logic and provisioning a scheduled compute resource, which is significantly more development effort than simply enabling TTL on the existing attribute.

question: A developer is creating a simple proof-of-concept demo by using AWS CloudFormation and AWS Lambda functions. The demo will use a CloudFormation template to deploy an existing Lambda function. The Lambda function uses deployment packages and dependencies stored in Amazon S3. The developer defined an AWS::Lambda::Function resource in a CloudFormation template. The developer needs to add the S3 bucket to the CloudFormation template. What should the developer do to meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Add the function code in the CloudFormation template inline as the code property.
Add the function code in the CloudFormation template as the ZipFile property.
Find the S3 key for the Lambda function. Add the S3 key as the ZipFile property in the CloudFormation template.
Add the relevant key and bucket to the S3Bucket and S3Key properties in the CloudFormation template.

explanation: The AWS::Lambda::Function resource's Code property accepts S3Bucket and S3Key sub-properties that point CloudFormation directly at the existing deployment package already stored in S3, requiring no code duplication or extra packaging step. The ZipFile property is meant for small amounts of inline source code embedded directly in the template (limited to a few KB, plain code text, not an S3 reference), so using it to hold an 'S3 key' is not valid. Putting the function code inline as a generic 'code property' isn't how the resource schema works; Code must use one of its defined sub-properties like S3Bucket/S3Key or ZipFile.

question: A developer is building a microservices-based application by using Python on AWS and several AWS services. The developer must use AWS X-Ray. The developer views the service map by using the console to view the service dependencies. During testing, the developer notices that some services are missing from the service map. What can the developer do to ensure that all services appear in the X-Ray service map?

options.text: Modify the X-Ray Python agent configuration in each service to increase the sampling rate.
Instrument the application by using the X-Ray SDK for Python. Install the X-Ray SDK for all the services that the application uses.
Enable X-Ray data aggregation in Amazon CloudWatch Logs for all the services that the application uses.
Increase the X-Ray service map timeout value in the X-Ray console.

explanation: The X-Ray service map is built from trace segments that each instrumented service sends to X-Ray, so any service missing from the map simply hasn't been instrumented to emit those traces yet; installing and configuring the X-Ray SDK for Python in every service that makes up the application ensures each one reports its segments and appears on the map. Adjusting the sampling rate only changes how many of the traces that are already being sent get recorded, it doesn't cause an uninstrumented service to start sending traces at all. There is no 'X-Ray data aggregation' setting in CloudWatch Logs, and increasing a service map timeout value is not a real X-Ray console feature.

question: A developer is building a containerized application on AWS. The application communicates with a third-party service by using API keys. The developer needs a secure way to store the API keys and pass the API keys to the containerized application. Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Store the API keys as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Grant the application access to retrieve the value from Parameter Store.
Store the API keys in AWS CloudFormation templates by using base64 encoding. Pass the API keys to the application through container definition environment variables.
Add a new AWS CloudFormation parameter to the CloudFormation template. Pass the API keys to the application by using the container definition environment variables.
Embed the API keys in the application. Build the container image on-premises. Upload the container image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
Store the API keys as a SecretString parameter in AWS Secrets Manager. Grant the application access to retrieve the value from Secrets Manager.

explanation: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameters and AWS Secrets Manager SecretString secrets both encrypt the API keys at rest using KMS and can be retrieved by the containerized application at runtime through IAM permissions, avoiding ever hardcoding the keys in the image or template. Base64-encoding a value in a CloudFormation template or environment variable is not encryption, it's trivially reversible and the value would still appear in template/task-definition metadata. Embedding the keys directly in the application code and baking them into the container image means the secret is permanently exposed in the image layers and in ECR, which is the opposite of secure storage.

question: A company runs an application on AWS. The application stores data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Some queries are taking a long time to run. These slow queries involve an attribute that is not the table's partition key or sort key. The amount of data that the application stores in the DynamoDB table is expected to increase significantly. A developer must increase the performance of the queries. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase the page size for each request by setting the Limit parameter to be higher than the default value. Configure the application to retry any request that exceeds the provisioned throughput.
Create a global secondary index (GSI). Set query attribute to be the partition key of the index.
Perform a parallel scan operation by issuing individual scan requests. In the parameters, specify the segment for the scan requests and the total number of segments for the parallel scan.
Turn on read capacity auto scaling for the DynamoDB table. Increase the maximum read capacity units (RCUs).

explanation: A global secondary index (GSI) lets you define a new partition key (and optional sort key) on a non-key attribute, allowing DynamoDB to serve queries on that attribute efficiently via the index rather than an expensive full table scan, and this approach scales well as the table grows. Increasing page size or read capacity does not change the fact that querying a non-key attribute still requires a scan of the base table, so those options only mask the underlying inefficiency and get more expensive as data grows. A parallel scan speeds up scanning the whole table but is still fundamentally a scan operation, consuming far more read capacity than an indexed query and not a real long-term fix for query performance.

question: A company runs a payment application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balance. The EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The application needs to retrieve application secrets during the application startup and export the secrets as environment variables. These secrets must be encrypted at rest and need to be rotated every month. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Save the secrets in a text file and store the text file in Amazon S3. Provision a customer managed key. Use the key for secret encryption in Amazon S3. Read the contents of the text file and read the export as environment variables. Configure S3 Object Lambda to rotate the text file every month.

Save the secrets as strings in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and use the default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Configure an Amazon EC2 user data script to retrieve the secrets during the startup and export as environment variables. Configure an AWS Lambda function to rotate the secrets in Parameter Store every month.

Save the secrets as base64 encoded environment variables in the application properties. Retrieve the secrets during the application startup. Reference the secrets in the application code. Write a script to rotate the secrets saved as environment variables.

Store the secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Provision a new customer master key. Use the key to encrypt the secrets. Enable automatic rotation. Configure an Amazon EC2 user data script to programmatically retrieve the secrets during the startup and export as environment variables.

explanation: AWS Secrets Manager stores the secrets encrypted at rest with a customer-managed KMS key, natively supports automatic monthly rotation, and the EC2 user data script can call the Secrets Manager API at instance startup to retrieve the current secret values and export them as environment variables, all with minimal custom code. Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameters can be encrypted, but Parameter Store itself has no built-in rotation, requiring the developer to build and maintain a separate Lambda function for rotation. Base64-encoded environment variables provide no real encryption, and S3 with a custom text file and 'S3 Object Lambda' rotation is not a real or appropriate mechanism for rotating secrets on a schedule.

question: A company is using Amazon API Gateway to invoke a new AWS Lambda function. The company has Lambda function versions in its PROD and DEV environments. In each environment, there is a Lambda function alias pointing to the corresponding Lambda function version. API Gateway has one stage that is configured to point at the PROD alias. The company wants to configure API Gateway to enable the PROD and DEV Lambda function versions to be simultaneously and distinctly available. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable a Lambda authorizer for the Lambda function alias in API Gateway. Republish PROD and create a new stage for DEV. Create API Gateway stage variables for the PROD and DEV stages. Point each stage variable to the PROD Lambda authorizer to the DEV Lambda authorizer.
Set up a gateway response in API Gateway for the Lambda function alias. Republish PROD and create a new stage for DEV. Create gateway responses in API Gateway for PROD and DEV Lambda aliases.

Use an environment variable for the Lambda function alias in API Gateway. Republish PROD and create a new stage for development. Create API gateway environment variables for PROD and DEV stages. Point each stage variable to the PROD Lambda function alias to the DEV Lambda function alias.

Use an API Gateway stage variable to configure the Lambda function alias. Republish PROD and create a new stage for development. Create API Gateway stage variables for PROD and DEV stages. Point each stage variable to the PROD Lambda function alias and to the DEV Lambda function alias.

explanation: API Gateway stage variables can hold the name of the Lambda function alias to invoke, and by republishing the PROD stage and creating a new DEV stage, each stage's variable can point to its corresponding alias (PROD alias vs. DEV alias), letting both versions be invoked simultaneously and distinctly through their own stage URLs. There is no 'environment variable' concept for API Gateway integrations (that's a Lambda function feature, not an API Gateway stage feature), so that option is not valid. Gateway responses customize API Gateway's own error output and Lambda authorizers control access; neither mechanism is used to route a stage to a specific Lambda alias/version.

question: A developer is working on an ecommerce platform that communicates with several third-party payment processing APIs. The third-party payment services do not provide a test environment. The developer needs to validate the ecommerce platform's integration with the third-party payment processing APIs. The developer must test the API integration code without invoking the third-party payment processing APIs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a gateway response configured for status code 200. Add response templates that contain sample responses captured from the real third-party API.

Set up an AWS AppSync GraphQL API with a data source configured for each third-party API. Specify an integration type of Mock. Configure integration responses by using sample responses captured from the real third-party API.

Create an AWS Lambda function for each third-party API. Embed responses captured from the real third-party API. Configure Amazon Route 53 Resolver with an inbound endpoint for each Lambda function's Amazon Resource Name (ARN).

Set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API for each third-party API. Specify an integration request type of Mock. Configure integration responses by using sample responses captured from the real third-party API.

explanation: API Gateway's mock integration type returns a configured response directly from API Gateway itself, without ever calling a backend, letting the developer simulate each third-party payment API's expected responses using captured sample data so the integration code can be tested end-to-end without touching the real (and test-environment-less) third-party services. AppSync's mock integration is a similar concept but is designed for GraphQL APIs, and this scenario uses REST-style API integrations for third-party services, not a GraphQL API being built by the company. Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints are for hybrid DNS resolution and have no role in mocking HTTP API responses, and gateway responses only customize API Gateway's own built-in error output rather than arbitrary integration responses.

question: A developer is storing many objects in a single Amazon S3 bucket. The developer needs to optimize the S3 bucket for high request rates. How should the developer store the objects to meet this requirement?

options.text: Store the objects by using S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
Store the objects at the root of the S3 bucket.
Store the objects by using object key names distributed across multiple prefixes.
Store each object with an object tag named "prefix" that contains a unique value.

explanation: S3 automatically partitions bucket data based on key name prefixes, so distributing objects across multiple different prefixes (rather than one flat namespace at the bucket root) allows S3 to spread the workload across more partitions and sustain a much higher aggregate request rate. Storing everything at the bucket root does not help distribute request load, since S3 still partitions by the shared prefix and can hit request-rate limits within that range. S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage cost by moving objects between access tiers; it does nothing to change how request throughput scales. Object tags are metadata used for filtering, lifecycle rules, and access control, not for influencing S3's internal request-rate partitioning.

question: A company deploys a new application to AWS. The company is streaming application logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The company's development team must receive notification by email when the word "ERROR" appears in any log lines. A developer sets up an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and subscribes the development team to the topic. What should the developer do next to meet the requirements?

options.text: Select the appropriate log group. Create a CloudWatch metric filter with "ERROR" as the search term. Create an alarm on this metric that notifies the SNS topic when the metric is 1 or higher.

In CloudWatch Logs Insights, select the appropriate log group. Create a metric query to search for the term "ERROR" in the logs. Create an alarm on this metric that notifies the SNS topic when the metric is 1 or higher.
Select the appropriate log group. Create an SNS subscription filter with "ERROR" as the filter pattern. Select the SNS topic as the destination.
Create a CloudWatch alarm that includes "ERROR" as a filter pattern, a log group dimension that defines the appropriate log group, and a destination that notifies the SNS topic.

explanation: A CloudWatch Logs metric filter can scan incoming log events for the literal term 'ERROR' and increment a custom metric each time it matches, and a CloudWatch alarm on that metric (triggering when the value reaches 1) can notify the existing SNS topic, which is exactly the alarm-driven, no-code path from log content to email notification. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries are for interactive/ad hoc analysis and don't natively produce a metric that CloudWatch alarms can act on the way metric filters do. An SNS subscription filter policy filters which messages an existing subscriber receives from messages already published to the topic, it cannot scan CloudWatch Logs content directly. A CloudWatch alarm needs a pre-existing metric to act on; it cannot use a raw text filter pattern as its trigger condition on its own without a metric filter first.

question: A company uses Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to decouple its microservices architecture. Some messages in an SQS queue contain sensitive information. A developer must implement a solution that encrypts all the data at rest. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable server-side encryption for the SQS queue by using an SQS managed encryption key (SSE-SQS).
Use the aws:SecureTransport condition in the queue policy to ensure that only HTTPS (TLS) is used for all requests to the SQS queue.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to generate an SSL/TLS certificate. Reference the certificate when messages are sent to the queue.
Set a message attribute in the SQS SendMessage request for messages that are sent to the queue. Set the Name to ENCRYPT. Set the Value to TRUE.

explanation: Enabling SQS server-side encryption (SSE) with an SQS-managed key (SSE-SQS) encrypts the message body while it is stored at rest in the queue, satisfying the requirement to protect sensitive message content at rest. Requiring aws:SecureTransport only enforces HTTPS/TLS for data in transit to and from the queue, it does not encrypt anything at rest. Referencing an ACM TLS certificate when sending messages also only secures the transport layer, not the stored message data. Setting a custom message attribute named ENCRYPT with value TRUE has no effect on SQS behavior; it does not trigger any actual encryption.

question: A company recently deployed a new serverless user portal. Users have reported that part of the portal is slow. The initial analysis found a single Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is responsible for the performance issues. The endpoint integrates with an AWS Lambda function. However, the Lambda function interacts with other APIs and AWS services. How can a developer find the source of the increased response time by using operational best practices?

options.text: Update the Lambda function by adding logging statements with high-precision timestamps before and after each external request. Deploy the updated Lambda function. After accumulating enough usage data, examine the Amazon CloudWatch logs for the Lambda function to determine the likely sources for the increased response time.

Instrument the Lambda function with the AWS X-Ray SDK. Add HTTP and HTTPS interceptors and SDK client handlers. Deploy the updated Lambda function. Turn on X-Ray tracing. After accumulating enough usage data, use the X-Ray service map to examine the average response times to determine the likely sources.

Review the Lambda function's Amazon CloudWatch metrics by using the metrics explorer. Apply anomaly detection to the Duration metric and the Throttles metric. Review the anomalies to determine the likely sources.

Use Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics to create a new canary. Turn on AWS X-Ray tracing on the canary. Configure the canary to scan the user portal. After accumulating enough usage data, use the CloudWatch Synthetics canary dashboard to view the metrics from the canary.

explanation: AWS X-Ray is purpose-built for tracing requests across distributed components, and instrumenting the Lambda function with the X-Ray SDK (including HTTP/HTTPS interceptors and AWS SDK client handlers) captures timing data for every downstream call the function makes. The resulting service map visually breaks down average response times per segment, letting the developer pinpoint exactly which downstream API or service is adding latency. Manually adding timestamped log statements (option A) works but is far more labor-intensive and error-prone to analyze at scale, CloudWatch anomaly detection on Duration/Throttles (option C) only flags that something is wrong without showing where, and a Synthetics canary (option D) tests availability/performance from the outside but doesn't decompose internal call latency the way X-Ray traces do.

question: A developer is building an event-driven application by using AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge. The Lambda function needs to push events to an EventBridge event bus. The developer uses an SDK to run the PutEvents EventBridge action and specifies no credentials in the code. After deploying the Lambda function, the developer notices that the function is failing and there are AccessDeniedException errors in the logs. How should the developer resolve this issue?

options.text: Configure a VPC peering connection between the Lambda function and EventBridge.
Modify their AWS credentials to include permissions for the PutEvents EventBridge action.
Modify the Lambda function execution role to include permissions for the PutEvents EventBridge action.
Add a resource-based policy to the Lambda function to include permissions for the PutEvents EventBridge action.

explanation: When a Lambda function calls an AWS API without hardcoded credentials, the SDK automatically uses the function's execution role to sign requests, so an AccessDeniedException means that role lacks the required permission. The fix is to add the events:PutEvents permission to the Lambda execution role's IAM policy, not to modify unrelated developer credentials. Resource-based policies on the Lambda function control who can invoke the function, not what the function itself can do, and VPC peering has nothing to do with IAM authorization for the EventBridge API call.

question: A company's application has an AWS Lambda function that processes messages from IoT devices. The company wants to monitor the Lambda function to ensure that the Lambda function is meeting its required service level agreement (SLA). A developer must implement a solution to determine the application's throughput in near real time. The throughput must be based on the number of messages that the Lambda function receives and processes in a given time period. The Lambda function performs initialization and post-processing steps that must not factor into the throughput measurement. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use the Lambda function's ConcurrentExecutions metric in Amazon CloudWatch to measure the throughput.
Modify the application to log the calculated throughput to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke a separate Lambda function to process the logs on a schedule.
Modify the application to publish custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics when the Lambda function receives and processes each message. Use the metrics to calculate the throughput.
Use the Lambda function's Invocations metric and Duration metric to calculate the throughput in Amazon CloudWatch.

explanation: Publishing custom CloudWatch metrics at the precise points where message processing begins and ends lets the developer measure only the actual processing time, deliberately excluding Lambda initialization (cold start) and post-processing overhead from the throughput calculation. This gives accurate, near-real-time throughput data because the metric emission happens inline with the business logic. Built-in metrics like Invocations, Duration, and ConcurrentExecutions reflect the entire invocation lifecycle and can't be scoped to exclude initialization/post-processing, and routing logs through a separate scheduled Lambda adds unnecessary latency and complexity for a near-real-time requirement.

question: A developer is using an AWS CodePipeline pipeline to provide continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) support for a Java application. The developer needs to update the pipeline to support the introduction of a new application dependency .jar file. The pipeline must start a build when a new version of the .jar file becomes available. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the dependency .jar file. Publish the dependency .jar file to the S3 bucket. Use an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to start a CodePipeline pipeline build.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) private repository. Publish the dependency .jar file to the repository. Use an ECR source action to start a CodePipeline pipeline build.

Create an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) private repository. Publish the dependency .jar file to the repository. Use an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to start a CodePipeline pipeline build.
Create an AWS CodeArtifact repository. Publish the dependency .jar file to the repository. Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to start a CodePipeline pipeline build.

explanation: AWS CodeArtifact is designed to host application dependencies (like .jar packages) and natively emits events to Amazon EventBridge whenever a new package version is published. Creating an EventBridge rule that matches these CodeArtifact package-version events and targets the CodePipeline pipeline lets the pipeline start automatically the moment a new dependency version becomes available. Amazon ECR is meant for container images, not language-level dependency artifacts, and S3 combined with SNS notifications is a workable but non-purpose-built pattern that CodeArtifact's native event integration handles more directly.

question: A company with multiple branch locations has an analytics and reporting application. Each branch office pushes a sales report to a shared Amazon S3 bucket at a predefined time each day. The company has developed an AWS Lambda function that analyzes the reports from all branch offices in a single pass. The Lambda function stores the results in a database. The company needs to start the analysis once each day at a specific time. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification to invoke the Lambda function when a branch office uploads a sales report.
Create an AWS Step Functions state machine that invokes the Lambda function once each day at the predefined time.
Configure the Lambda function to run continuously and to begin analysis only at the predefined time each day.
Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule that invokes the Lambda function once each day at the predefined time.

explanation: An Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule (using a cron or rate expression) is the most cost-effective way to invoke a Lambda function at a specific time once per day, since it only triggers the function exactly when needed and incurs no cost between invocations. Running the Lambda function continuously (option C) would waste compute and incur ongoing charges, and standing up a Step Functions state machine just to invoke the function on a schedule (option B) adds unnecessary orchestration cost and complexity for a single scheduled task. S3 event notifications (option A) would trigger analysis on every individual upload rather than once daily as required.

question: A developer has an application that asynchronously invokes an AWS Lambda function. The developer wants to store messages that resulted in failed invocations of the Lambda function so that the application can retry the call later. What should the developer do to accomplish this goal with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Set up Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups to filter and store the messages in an Amazon S3 bucket. Import the messages in Lambda. Run the Lambda function again.
Configure Amazon EventBridge to send the messages to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to initiate the Lambda function again.
Implement a dead-letter queue for discarded messages. Set the dead-letter queue as an event source for the Lambda function.
Send Amazon EventBridge events to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the Lambda function to pull messages from the SQS queue. Run the Lambda function again.

explanation: For asynchronous Lambda invocations, AWS lets you configure a dead-letter queue (an SQS queue or SNS topic) directly on the function to automatically capture the event payload after all retry attempts are exhausted, with no custom code required. This is the lowest-overhead solution because Lambda handles the retry-then-forward logic natively; the application can later reprocess messages from the DLQ. Filtering CloudWatch Logs and re-importing events, or manually routing through EventBridge/SNS/SQS to reinvoke the function, both require custom plumbing that a native DLQ configuration avoids entirely.

question: A company is using AWS CloudFormation templates to deploy AWS resources. The company needs to update one of its AWS CloudFormation stacks. What can the company do to find out how the changes will impact the resources that are running?

options.text: Investigate the change sets.
Investigate the stack policies.
Investigate the Metadata section.
Investigate the Resources section.

explanation: A CloudFormation change set generates a preview of exactly which resources will be added, modified, or replaced (and whether a modification requires replacement) before the update is actually applied to the running stack. This lets the developer assess impact and risk safely ahead of time. Stack policies control which update actions are permitted (a preventive control, not a preview mechanism), while the Metadata and Resources sections of a template just describe the desired end state and don't show the delta against what's currently deployed.

question: A company stores all personally identifiable information (PII) in an Amazon DynamoDB table named PII in Account A. Developers are working on an application that is running on Amazon EC2 instances in Account B. The application in Account B requires access to the PII table. An administrator in Account A creates an IAM role named AccessPII that has permission to access the PII table. The administrator also creates a trust policy that specifies Account B as a principal that can assume the role. Which combination of steps should the developers take in Account B to allow their application to access the PII table? (Choose two.)

options.text: Allow the EC2 IAM role the permission to assume the AccessPII role.
Allow the EC2 IAM role the permission to access the PII table.
Include the AWS API in the application code logic to obtain temporary credentials from the EC2 IAM role to access the PII table.
Include the AssumeRole API operation in the application code logic to obtain temporary credentials to access the PII table.
Include the GetSessionToken API operation in the application code logic to obtain temporary credentials to access the PII table.

explanation: For cross-account access, the EC2 instance's own IAM role in Account B needs an attached policy granting it permission to call sts:AssumeRole on the AccessPII role in Account A, and the application code needs to actually invoke the AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials scoped to that role. The application then uses those temporary credentials (not the instance's own permissions) to access the DynamoDB table, since the underlying EC2 role itself has no direct access to the table. GetSessionToken only refreshes credentials for the calling identity's own permissions and cannot be used to assume a different role, and granting the EC2 role direct table access would bypass the cross-account trust relationship the administrator already set up.

question: A gaming website gives users the ability to trade game items with each other on the platform. The platform requires both users' records to be updated and persisted in one transaction. If any update fails, the transaction must roll back. Which AWS solutions can provide the transactional capability that is required for this feature? (Choose two.)

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB with operations made with the ConsistentRead parameter set to true
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with operations made within a transaction block
Amazon DynamoDB with reads and writes made by using Transact* operations
Amazon Aurora MySQL with operations made within a transaction block
Amazon Athena with operations made within a transaction block

explanation: DynamoDB Transact* operations (TransactWriteItems/TransactGetItems) provide true ACID transactions across multiple items, guaranteeing that either all writes succeed or none do, which satisfies the all-or-nothing rollback requirement. Amazon Aurora MySQL, being a relational database, natively supports multi-statement transactions wrapped in BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK blocks. Setting ConsistentRead on regular DynamoDB operations only affects read consistency, not transactional writes, and neither ElastiCache for Memcached nor Amazon Athena offer ACID transaction semantics for this kind of coordinated multi-record update.

question: A developer is deploying an application in the AWS Cloud by using AWS CloudFormation. The application will connect to an existing Amazon RDS database. The hostname of the RDS database is stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a plaintext value. The developer needs to incorporate the database hostname into the CloudFormation template to initialize the application when the stack is created. How should the developer reference the parameter that contains the database hostname?

options.text: Use the ssm dynamic reference.
Use the Ref intrinsic function.
Use the Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function.
Use the ssm-secure dynamic reference.

explanation: CloudFormation dynamic references let a template pull a value from another AWS service at deployment/update time without hardcoding it, and the {{resolve:ssm:parameter-name:version}} pattern is specifically used to retrieve plaintext String or StringList parameters from Systems Manager Parameter Store. The ssm-secure dynamic reference is reserved for SecureString parameters, which doesn't apply here since the hostname is stored as plaintext. Ref only resolves logical resource IDs or parameters declared within the same template, and Fn::ImportValue only retrieves values explicitly exported by another CloudFormation stack's Outputs section — neither applies to a value stored in Parameter Store.

question: A company uses an AWS Lambda function to call a third-party service. The third-party service has a limit of requests each minute. If the number of requests exceeds the limit, the third-party service returns rate-limiting errors. A developer needs to configure the Lambda function to avoid receiving rate limiting errors from the third-party service. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Set the reserved concurrency on the Lambda function to match the number of concurrent requests that the third-party service allows.
Decrease the memory that is allocated to the Lambda function.
Set the provisioned concurrency on the Lambda function to match the number of concurrent requests that the third-party service allows.
Increase the timeout value that is specified on the Lambda function.

explanation: Setting reserved concurrency caps the maximum number of concurrent executions for the Lambda function, which directly throttles how many simultaneous calls can go out to the rate-limited third-party service, preventing the function from exceeding the service's per-minute limit. Provisioned concurrency only pre-initializes execution environments to reduce cold starts and does not cap maximum concurrency, so it wouldn't prevent overwhelming the third-party API. Adjusting memory or timeout settings affects execution speed or how long a single invocation can run, but neither controls how many requests are fired concurrently at the downstream service.

question: A developer is building a new containerized application by using AWS Copilot. The developer uses the AWS Copilot command line interface (CLI) to deploy the application during development. The developer committed the application code to a new AWS CodeCommit repository. The developer must create an automated deployment process before releasing the new application to production. What should the developer do to meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Create a buildspec file that invokes the AWS Copilot CLI commands to build and deploy the application. Use the AWS Copilot CLI to create an AWS CodePipeline that uses the CodeCommit repository in the source stage and AWS CodeBuild in the build stage.

Use the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI to bootstrap and initialize an AWS CodePipeline configuration. Use the CodeCommit repository as the source. Invoke the AWS Copilot CLI to build and deploy the application.
Use the AWS Copilot CLI to define the AWS Copilot pipeline and to deploy the AWS CodePipeline. Select CodeCommit as the source for the AWS CodePipeline.
Define an AWS CloudFormation template for an AWS CodePipeline with CodeCommit as the source. Configure the template as an AWS Copilot CLI add-on. Use the AWS Copilot CLI to deploy the application.

explanation: AWS Copilot has built-in pipeline commands (copilot pipeline init and copilot pipeline deploy) that automatically generate and provision a fully configured CodePipeline — including a CodeCommit source stage, build, and deploy stages tailored to the containerized application — without the developer needing to hand-write CloudFormation templates or buildspec files. This is the most operationally efficient path because it reuses Copilot's existing knowledge of the application's environment and deployment topology. The other options involve manually assembling pipeline configuration (via CloudFormation, SAM CLI, or custom buildspecs) that duplicates work Copilot already automates natively.

question: A developer is creating a new application for a pet store. The application will manage customer rewards points. The developer will use Amazon DynamoDB to store the data for the application. The developer needs to optimize query performance and limit partition overload before actual performance analysis. Which option should the developer use for a partition key to meet these requirements?

options.text: A randomly generated universally unique identifier (UUID)
The customer's full name
The date when the customer signed up for the rewards program
The name of the customer's pet

explanation: A high-cardinality, randomly distributed value like a UUID spreads write and read traffic evenly across DynamoDB partitions, which is the standard technique for avoiding hot partitions before any real usage data exists to inform a more tailored strategy. Attributes like a customer's full name, signup date, or pet name are all low-cardinality or unevenly distributed (many customers could share a name, sign-up date, or common pet name), which risks concentrating traffic on a small number of partitions and degrading performance. A UUID (effectively a synthetic customer ID) is the safest default partition key choice for even distribution.

question: A company is building a serverless application. The application uses an API key to authenticate with a third-party application. The company wants to store the external API key as a part of an AWS Lambda configuration. The company needs to have full control over the AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys that will encrypt the API key and should be visible only to authorized entities. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the API key in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a string parameter. Use the default AWS KMS key that AWS provides to encrypt the API key.
Store the API key in AWS Lambda environment variables. Create an AWS KMS customer managed key to encrypt the API key.
Store the API key in the code repository. Use an AWS managed key to encrypt the code repository.
Store the API key as an Amazon DynamoDB table record. Use an AWS managed key to encrypt the API key.

explanation: Storing the API key as a Lambda environment variable and encrypting it with a customer managed KMS key gives the company full administrative control over the key — including key policies, rotation, and the ability to restrict which IAM principals can use it to decrypt the value — unlike the AWS managed or default service keys used in the other options, which the account owner cannot fully control. Lambda automatically encrypts environment variables at rest, and when a customer managed key is specified, the company can enforce granular access via the key policy so only authorized entities can decrypt the API key. Storing secrets in a code repository (even encrypted) is a poor practice since it mixes secrets with source code.

question: A developer is writing an application to analyze the traffic to a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances run behind a public Application Load Balancer (ALB). An HTTP server runs on each of the EC2 instances, logging all requests to a log file. The developer wants to capture the client public IP addresses. The developer analyzes the log files and notices only the IP address of the ALB. What must the developer do to capture the client public IP addresses in the log file?

options.text: Add a Host header to the HTTP server log configuration file.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch Logs agent on each EC2 instance. Configure the agent to write to the log file.
Install the AWS X-Ray daemon on each EC2 instance. Configure the daemon to write to the log file.
Add an X-Forwarded-For header to the HTTP server log configuration file.

explanation: An Application Load Balancer terminates client connections and forwards requests to backend targets from its own IP addresses, so without extra configuration, backend logs only show the ALB's IP rather than the original client's. ALBs automatically add an X-Forwarded-For header containing the original client IP to every forwarded request, so configuring the HTTP server to log that header's value recovers the true client IP address. Installing CloudWatch Logs agent or the X-Ray daemon addresses log shipping or distributed tracing, not the underlying problem of the client IP being replaced by the load balancer's IP in the first place.

question: A company is developing a serverless application by using AWS Lambda functions. One of the Lambda functions needs to access an Amazon RDS DB instance. The DB instance is in a private subnet inside a VPC. The company creates a role that includes the necessary permissions to access the DB instance. The company then assigns the role to the Lambda function. A developer must take additional action to give the Lambda function access to the DB instance. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Assign a public IP address to the DB instance. Modify the security group of the DB instance to allow inbound traffic from the IP address of the Lambda function.
Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the Lambda function and the DB instance.
Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution to create a secure connection between the Lambda function and the DB instance.
Configure the Lambda function to connect to the private subnets in the VPC. Add security group rules to allow traffic to the DB instance from the Lambda function.

explanation: By default, a Lambda function isn't attached to any VPC and cannot reach resources in a private subnet, so simply granting IAM permissions to the execution role isn't enough — network-level connectivity has to be configured too. The developer must configure the Lambda function's VPC settings to attach it to the relevant private subnets (which causes Lambda to provision elastic network interfaces there) and ensure security group rules allow traffic between the Lambda ENIs and the RDS instance's security group. Exposing the database publicly, using Direct Connect, or routing through CloudFront are all inappropriate and insecure ways to solve what is fundamentally a VPC networking configuration issue for a resource that should remain private.

question: A developer needs temporary access to resources in a second account. What is the MOST secure way to achieve this?

options.text: Use the Amazon Cognito user pools to get short-lived credentials for the second account.
Create a dedicated IAM access key for the second account, and send it by mail.
Create a cross-account access role, and use sts:AssumeRole API to get short-lived credentials.
Establish trust, and add an SSH key for the second account to the IAM user.

explanation: Creating a cross-account IAM role in the target account and having the developer's identity call sts:AssumeRole is the AWS-recommended pattern for secure, temporary cross-account access — it returns short-lived credentials that expire automatically and never requires distributing long-term secrets. Emailing an access key or attaching SSH keys to an IAM user both involve long-lived, easily leaked credentials that violate security best practices, and Cognito user pools are designed for authenticating end users of an application, not for granting a developer access to a separate AWS account's resources.

question: A company wants to migrate applications from its on-premises servers to AWS. As a first step, the company is modifying and migrating a non-critical application to a single Amazon EC2 instance. The application will store information in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to follow security best practices when deploying the application on AWS. Which approach should the company take to allow the application to interact with Amazon S3?

options.text: Create an IAM role that has administrative access to AWS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance.

Create an IAM user. Attach the AdministratorAccess policy. Copy the generated access key and secret key. Within the application code, use the access key and secret key along with the AWS SDK to communicate with Amazon S3.
Create an IAM role that has the necessary access to Amazon S3. Attach the role to the EC2 instance.

Create an IAM user. Attach a policy that provides the necessary access to Amazon S3. Copy the generated access key and secret key. Within the application code, use the access key and secret key along with the AWS SDK to communicate with Amazon S3.

explanation: Attaching an IAM role scoped only to the required S3 permissions to the EC2 instance follows the principle of least privilege and lets the AWS SDK automatically retrieve and rotate temporary credentials via the instance metadata service, with no secrets stored anywhere in the application. Using an administrative role or user grants far more access than the application needs, and creating an IAM user with long-lived access keys embedded in the application code is a security anti-pattern since those keys don't rotate automatically and can be exposed if the code or instance is compromised.

question: A company has an internal website that contains sensitive data. The company wants to make the website public. The company must ensure that only employees who authenticate through the company's OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider (IdP) can access the website. A developer needs to implement authentication without editing the website. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a public Network Load Balancer.
Create a public Application Load Balancer.
Configure a listener for the load balancer that listens on HTTPS port 443. Add a default authenticate action providing the OIDC IdP configuration.
Configure a listener for the load balancer that listens on HTTP port 80. Add a default authenticate action providing the OIDC IdP configuration.
Configure a listener for the load balancer that listens on HTTPS port 443. Add a default AWS Lambda action providing an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) to a Lambda authentication function.

explanation: An Application Load Balancer supports a built-in authenticate-oidc action on its listener rules, which integrates directly with an OpenID Connect identity provider to enforce authentication before requests ever reach the backend — requiring no changes to the website's own code. Because the site holds sensitive data, the listener should use HTTPS on port 443 (not unencrypted HTTP on port 80) so credentials and session tokens aren't exposed in transit. Network Load Balancers operate at the transport layer and don't support this authentication feature, and a custom Lambda authorizer action would require the developer to build custom authentication logic instead of using the ALB's native OIDC integration.

question: A developer is working on a web application that requires selective activation of specific features. The developer wants to keep the features hidden from end users until the features are ready for public access. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a feature flag configuration profile in AWS AppSync. Store the feature flag values in the configuration profile. Activate and deactivate feature flags as needed.
Store prerelease data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams in the table. Toggle between hidden and visible states by using DynamoDB Streams.
Create a feature flag configuration profile in AWS AppConfig. Store the feature flag values in the configuration profile. Activate and deactivate feature flags as needed.
Store prerelease data in AWS Amplify DataStore. Toggle between hidden and visible states by using Amplify DataStore cloud synchronization.

explanation: AWS AppConfig has a dedicated feature flag capability where a configuration profile stores flag values that can be toggled on or off independently of application deployments, letting the developer hide unfinished features from end users and activate them later without redeploying code. AppSync is a managed GraphQL service and has no feature-flag configuration profile concept. Using DynamoDB Streams or Amplify DataStore synchronization to toggle visibility would require building custom logic to interpret data changes as feature toggles, which is far more operational effort than AppConfig's purpose-built feature flag support.

question: A developer at a company writes an AWS CloudFormation template. The template refers to subnets that were created by a separate AWS CloudFormation template that the company's network team wrote. When the developer attempts to launch the stack for the first time, the launch fails. Which template coding mistakes could have caused this failure? (Choose two.)

options.text: The developer's template does not use the Ref intrinsic function to refer to the subnets.
The developer's template does not use the ImportValue intrinsic function to refer to the subnets.
The Mappings section of the developer's template does not refer to the subnets.
The network team's template does not export the subnets in the Outputs section.
The network team's template does not export the subnets in the Mappings section.

explanation: To share a resource like a subnet ID across separate CloudFormation stacks, the stack that creates the resource must export its value in the Outputs section, and the consuming template must retrieve it with the Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function — omitting either step breaks the cross-stack reference and causes the stack launch to fail. Ref only resolves values within the same template (it can't reach into another stack), and the Mappings section is used for static, pre-defined key-value lookups rather than for consuming values produced by another stack's resources.

question: A developer is running an application on an Amazon EC2 instance. When the application tries to read an Amazon S3 bucket, the application fails. The developer notices that the associated IAM role is missing the S3 read permission. The developer needs to give the application the ability to read the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST application disruption?

options.text: Add the permission to the role. Terminate the existing EC2 instance. Launch a new EC2 instance.
Add the permission to the role so that the change will take effect automatically.
Add the permission to the role. Hibernate and restart the existing EC2 instance.
Add the permission to the S3 bucket. Restart the EC2 instance.

explanation: IAM role and policy changes take effect within seconds to a couple of minutes and are automatically picked up by any credentials the EC2 instance retrieves afterward via the instance metadata service — there's no need to restart, hibernate, or replace the instance for a permission change to apply. Attaching the permission directly to the S3 bucket policy instead of the role, or unnecessarily cycling the instance, would add complexity and disruption that isn't required to resolve a simple missing-permission issue on the existing IAM role.

question: A developer is writing a web application that is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB). The developer must add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB. The developer also must ensure that customer data from outside the VPC is encrypted in transit. Which combination of CloudFront configuration settings should the developer use to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Restrict viewer access by using signed URLs.
Set the Origin Protocol Policy setting to Match Viewer.
Enable field-level encryption.
Enable automatic object compression.
Set the Viewer Protocol Policy setting to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

explanation: To ensure the entire path from viewer to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the ALB origin stays encrypted, the Viewer Protocol Policy should be set to redirect HTTP to HTTPS (forcing clients to use TLS) and the Origin Protocol Policy should be set to Match Viewer so CloudFront also connects to the origin over HTTPS when the viewer used HTTPS. Together these settings enforce encryption in transit end-to-end. Signed URLs control access authorization rather than encryption, field-level encryption protects specific sensitive form fields rather than the whole transit path, and object compression is purely a performance optimization unrelated to encryption.

question: A developer is implementing an AWS Lambda function that will be invoked when an object is uploaded to Amazon S3. The developer wants to test the Lambda function in a local development machine before publishing the function to a production AWS account. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Upload an object to Amazon S3 by using the aws s3api put-object CLI command. Wait for the local Lambda invocation from the S3 event.
Create a sample JSON text file for a put object S3 event. Invoke the Lambda function locally. Use the aws lambda invoke CLI command with the JSON file and Lambda function name as arguments.

Use the sam local start-lambda CLI command to start Lambda. Use the sam local generate-event s3 put CLI command to create the Lambda test JSON file. Use the sam local invoke CLI command with the JSON file as the argument to invoke the Lambda function.
Create a JSON string for the put object S3 event. In the AWS Management Console, use the JSON string to create a test event for the local Lambda function. Perform the test.

explanation: The AWS SAM CLI provides purpose-built local testing tools: sam local generate-event creates a realistic sample event payload (such as an S3 put-object event) and sam local invoke runs the Lambda function locally using that event, all without needing to deploy anything or wait for a real S3 upload to trigger the function. This combination gives the fastest, lowest-overhead local test loop. Actually uploading to S3 and waiting for invocation, hand-crafting JSON files for the CLI, or building test events in the console all require more manual setup and don't test purely on the local machine before publishing.

question: A developer is publishing critical log data to a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The log group was created 2 months ago. The developer must encrypt the log data by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key so that future data can be encrypted to comply with the company's security policy. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Use the AWS Encryption SDK for encryption and decryption of the data before writing to the log group.
Use the AWS KMS console to associate the KMS key with the log group.
Use the AWS CLI aws logs create-log-group command, and specify the key Amazon Resource Name (ARN).
Use the AWS CLI aws logs associate-kms-key command, and specify the key Amazon Resource Name (ARN).

explanation: The aws logs associate-kms-key CLI command lets you attach a KMS key to an existing CloudWatch Logs log group after the fact, encrypting all log data written to it going forward, which is exactly what's needed since the log group already exists and was created without encryption. The create-log-group command with a key ARN only applies at group creation time and can't be used to retroactively add encryption to an existing group, and there's no way to associate a KMS key with an existing log group directly through the KMS console — CloudWatch Logs owns that association. The AWS Encryption SDK would require rewriting application code to manually encrypt/decrypt each log entry, adding unnecessary effort.

question: A developer is building an ecommerce application. When there is a sale event, the application needs to concurrently call three third-party systems to record the sale. The developer wrote three AWS Lambda functions. There is one Lambda function for each third-party system, which contains complex integration logic. These Lambda functions are all independent. The developer needs to design the application so each Lambda function will run regardless of others' success or failure. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Publish the sale event from the application to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the three Lambda functions to poll the queue.
Publish the sale event from the application to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the three Lambda functions to be triggered by the SNS topic.
Publish the sale event from the application to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Add the three Lambda functions as ALB targets.
Publish the sale event from the application to an AWS Step Functions state machine. Move the logic from the three Lambda functions into the Step Functions state machine.

explanation: Amazon SNS supports fan-out, where a single published message is delivered independently to every subscriber, so all three Lambda functions receive and process the same sale event in parallel, and a failure in one subscriber's processing has no effect on the delivery or execution of the others. An SQS queue, by contrast, delivers each message to only one consumer (unless paired with separate queues per subscriber), which wouldn't let all three functions independently process the same event. An ALB is designed to route HTTP traffic to a single target per request, not fan out an event to multiple independent Lambda functions, and moving the logic into a single Step Functions state machine would couple the three integrations together rather than keeping them as independent, resilient functions.

question: A developer is writing an application, which stores data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The developer wants to query the DynamoDB table by using the partition key and a different sort key value. The developer needs the latest data with all recent write operations. How should the developer write the DynamoDB query?

options.text: Add a local secondary index (LSI) during table creation. Query the LSI by using eventually consistent reads.
Add a local secondary index (LSI) during table creation. Query the LSI by using strongly consistent reads.
Add a global secondary index (GSI) during table creation. Query the GSI by using eventually consistent reads.
Add a global secondary index (GSI) during table creation. Query the GSI by using strongly consistent reads.

explanation: Local secondary indexes share the same partition key as the base table while offering an alternate sort key, which matches the requirement of querying with the partition key plus a different sort key, and LSIs are the only DynamoDB index type that can serve strongly consistent reads (needed here to see the latest write). Global secondary indexes only ever return eventually consistent results, since GSI updates are propagated asynchronously from the base table.

question: A developer manages an application that writes customer orders to an Amazon DynamoDB table. The orders use customer_id as the partition key, order_id as the sort key, and order_date as an attribute. A new access pattern requires accessing data by order_date and order_id. The developer needs to implement a new AWS Lambda function to support the new access pattern. How should the developer support the new access pattern in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Add a new local secondary index (LSI) to the DynamoDB table that specifies order_date as the partition key and order_id as the sort key. Write the new Lambda function to query the new LSI index.
Write the new Lambda function to scan the DynamoDB table. In the Lambda function, write a method to retrieve and combine results by order_date and order_id.
Add a new global secondary index (GSI) to the DynamoDB table that specifies order_date as the partition key and order_id as the sort key. Write the new Lambda function to query the new GSI index.
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table. Choose the new and old images information to write to the DynamoDB stream. Write the new Lambda function to query the DynamoDB stream

explanation: A global secondary index lets the developer define an entirely new partition key (order_date) and sort key (order_id) that differ from the base table's key schema (customer_id/order_id), which is required here since the new access pattern needs to query by order_date as the leading key. A local secondary index can't satisfy this because an LSI must always retain the base table's original partition key (customer_id), so it can't be queried by order_date as a primary lookup key. Scanning the whole table or trying to repurpose DynamoDB Streams (which reflects change events, not a queryable index) would be far less efficient than a purpose-built GSI.

question: A developer is creating a web application for a school that stores data in Amazon DynamoDB. The ExamScores table has the following attributes: student_id, subject_name, and top_score. Each item in the ExamScores table is identified with student_id as the partition key and subject_name as the sort key. The web application needs to display the student _id for the top scores for each school subject. The developer needs to increase the speed of the queries to retrieve the student_id for the top scorer for each school subject. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a local secondary index (LSI) with subject_name as the partition key and top_score as the sort key.
Create a local secondary index (LSI) with top_score as the partition key and student_id as the sort key.
Create a global secondary index (GSI) with subject_name as the partition key and top_score as the sort key.
Create a global secondary index (GSI) with subject_name as the partition key and student_id as the sort key.

explanation: A global secondary index with subject_name as the partition key and top_score as the sort key lets the application query all scores for a subject sorted by score, making it fast to retrieve the top scorer per subject. This works because a GSI can define a completely new partition key that differs from the base table's partition key (student_id), whereas a local secondary index must keep student_id as its partition key and therefore couldn't group and sort results by subject_name across different students. Options B's LSI structure (top_score as partition key) is also invalid since LSIs must share the base table's partition key.

question: A developer is creating an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. The messages represent customer data updates from a customer relationship management (CRM) system The developer wants the Lambda function to process only the messages that pertain to email address changes. Additional subscribers to the SNS topic will process any other messages. Which solution will meet these requirements in the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Use Lambda event filtering to allow only messages that are related to email address changes to invoke the Lambda function.
Use an SNS filter policy on the Lambda function subscription to allow only messages that are related to email address changes to invoke the Lambda function.

Subscribe an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to the SNS topic. Configure the SQS queue with a filter policy to allow only messages that are related to email address changes. Connect the SQS queue to the Lambda function.

Configure the Lambda code to check the received message. If the message is not related to an email address change, configure the Lambda function to publish the message back to the SNS topic for the other subscribers to process.

explanation: SNS subscription filter policies let a subscriber declare, at the subscription level, which message attributes it wants delivered — so the Lambda function's subscription can be filtered to only receive messages tagged as email address changes, with SNS handling the filtering natively before invoking the function. This requires no custom code in the Lambda function itself, unlike checking and re-publishing unwanted messages in the function body (option D), which also risks message loops. Lambda's own event filtering feature applies to event sources like DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis, and SQS, not to direct SNS subscriptions, and adding an SQS queue as an intermediary is unnecessary extra infrastructure when SNS filter policies solve this directly.

question: A developer is designing a fault-tolerant environment where client sessions will be saved. How can the developer ensure that no sessions are lost if an Amazon EC2 instance fails?

options.text: Use sticky sessions with an Elastic Load Balancer target group.
Use Amazon SQS to save session data.
Use Amazon DynamoDB to perform scalable session handling.
Use Elastic Load Balancer connection draining to stop sending requests to failing instances.

explanation: Storing session data in Amazon DynamoDB decouples the session state from any individual EC2 instance, so if an instance fails, the session data remains intact and accessible from any other instance handling subsequent requests. Sticky sessions bind a client to one specific instance and offer no protection against data loss if that instance fails — the opposite of what's needed here. SQS is a message queue meant for decoupling asynchronous workloads, not for storing and querying session state, and connection draining only manages in-flight requests during instance deregistration, it doesn't preserve session data itself.

question: A developer is creating AWS CloudFormation templates to manage an application's deployment in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) through AWS CodeDeploy. The developer wants to automatically deploy new versions of the application to a percentage of users before the new version becomes available for all users. How should the developer manage the deployment of the new version?

options.text: Modify the CloudFormation template to include a Transform section and the AWS::CodeDeploy::BlueGreen hook.
Deploy the new version in a new CloudFormation stack. After testing is complete, update the application's DNS records for the new stack.
Run CloudFormation stack updates on the application stack to deploy new application versions when they are available.
Create a nested stack for the new version. Include a Transform section and the AWS::CodeDeploy::BlueGreen hook.

explanation: The AWS::CodeDeploy::BlueGreen CloudFormation hook, declared alongside a Transform section, natively integrates CodeDeploy blue/green deployment logic into a CloudFormation stack update for ECS services, enabling controlled traffic shifting (including canary/linear percentage-based rollout) to the new task set before it becomes available to all users. Simply running ordinary stack updates (option C) would just replace the service directly with no gradual traffic shifting. Deploying to an entirely separate stack and manually cutting over DNS (option B) is a much more manual, error-prone approach, and wrapping the hook in a nested stack (option D) adds unnecessary complexity since the hook can be applied directly to the main template.

question: A developer has written a distributed application that uses microservices. The microservices are running on Amazon EC2 instances. Because of message volume, the developer is unable to match log output from each microservice to a specific transaction. The developer needs to analyze the message flow to debug the application. Which combination of steps should the developer take to meet this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Download the AWS X-Ray daemon. Install the daemon on an EC2 instance. Ensure that the EC2 instance allows UDP traffic on port 2000.
Configure an interface VPC endpoint to allow traffic to reach the global AWS X-Ray daemon on TCP port 2000.
Enable AWS X-Ray. Configure Amazon CloudWatch to push logs to X-Ray.
Add the AWS X-Ray software development kit (SDK) to the microservices. Use X-Ray to trace requests that each microservice makes.
Set up Amazon CloudWatch metric streams to collect streaming data from the microservices.

explanation: To trace a request end-to-end across multiple microservices, you need both the X-Ray daemon running on each EC2 instance (listening on UDP port 2000 to receive and relay trace segments to the X-Ray service) and the X-Ray SDK integrated into each microservice's code so that each service actually generates and forwards trace segments tied to a shared trace ID. Together these let the developer follow a single transaction's flow across services in the X-Ray console. CloudWatch Logs and metric streams can show volume and errors but can't correlate a single transaction across independently logging microservices the way X-Ray's trace IDs do, and there's no interface VPC endpoint mechanism for reaching a global X-Ray daemon since the daemon runs locally on each host.

question: A developer needs to modify an application architecture to meet new functional requirements. Application data is stored in Amazon DynamoDB and processed for analysis in a nightly batch. The system analysts do not want to wait until the next day to view the processed data and have asked to have it available in near-real time. Which application architecture pattern would enable the data to be processed as it is received?

options.text: Event driven
Client-server driven
Fan-out driven
Schedule driven

explanation: An event-driven architecture processes data as soon as it's produced — reacting to individual events (like a DynamoDB write) in near-real time — rather than waiting for a scheduled interval, which is exactly the shift needed to eliminate the nightly batch delay.
